text: Jean-Antoine Watteau (UK: /ˈwɒtoʊ/, US: /wɒˈtoʊ/; baptised 10 October 1684 – died 18 July 1721) was a French painter and draughtsman whose short career revitalized interest in colour and movement, echoing the traditions of Correggio and Rubens. He transformed the waning Baroque style into a more naturalistic, less formal, and less classical Rococo aesthetic. Watteau is credited with inventing the genre of fêtes galantes—idyllic, bucolic scenes imbued with theatricality—drawing inspiration from Italian comedy and ballet. Born in October 1684 in Valenciennes, a town once part of the County of Hainaut and later the Burgundian and Habsburg Netherlands before joining France after the Franco-Dutch War, he was the second of four sons of Jean-Philippe Watteau (1660–1720) and Michelle Lardenois (1653–1727), and is presumed to be of Walloon descent. The Watteau family was well-to-do, though Jean-Philippe, a roofer, was known for brawling. Showing early interest in painting, Watteau may have apprenticed with local painter Jacques-Albert Gérin, initially painting scenes of street vendors selling quack remedies. He moved to Paris in 1702, worked as a scene-painter, and due to poor health, joined the workshop at Pont Notre-Dame, where he copied Flemish and Dutch genre paintings and developed his characteristic sketchlike technique. His drawings caught the attention of Claude Gillot, and by 1705 he became his assistant; in Gillot’s studio, he encountered the commedia dell'arte, a subject that became central to his work. After a dispute with Gillot, Watteau joined Claude Audran III’s workshop, where he developed elegant drawings and learned decorative art and ornamental design from Audran, the curator of the Palais du Luxembourg. There, he saw Rubens’s magnificent canvases for Queen Marie de Medici, a major influence, and later studied the works of Venetian masters in the collection of his patron and friend, banker Pierre Crozat. During this time, he painted *The Departing Regiment*, the first work in his more personal style influenced by Rubens and the first in a series of camp scenes; Audran dismissed it, prompting Watteau to return to Valenciennes, where he painted small camp pieces like *Camp-Fire*, sold first for 60 livres and later for 200 livres to Sirois, father-in-law of his future patron Edme-François Gersaint. In 1709, he attempted the Prix de Rome but won only second prize; in 1712, after being persuaded by Charles de La Fosse that Rome was unnecessary, he was accepted as an associate member of the Academy in 1712 and a full member in 1717, completing his required reception piece, *The Pilgrimage to Cythera* (also known as *The Embarkation for Cythera*). He later lived with Pierre Crozat, whose death in 1740 left around 400 paintings and 19,000 drawings, allowing Watteau further study of Rubens and the Venetian masters. Despite lacking aristocratic patrons, his buyers were bourgeois, including bankers and dealers; among his most famous works are two versions of *The Pilgrimage to Cythera* (one in the Louvre, one in Schloss Charlottenburg, Berlin), *Pierrot* (long identified as "Gilles"), *Fêtes venitiennes*, *Love in the Italian Theater*, *Love in the French Theater*, *"Voulez-vous triompher des belles?"*, and *Mezzetin*. *Pierrot* depicts an isolated actor in a white satin costume with an enigmatic expression. His final masterpiece, *The Shop-sign of Gersaint*, painted in eight days, only in the mornings to warm his fingers, shifts from pastoral settings to an urban scene and is seen as a meditation on art and illusion, comparable to *Las Meninas*. Watteau showed disregard for his future and finances, likely foreseeing his early death; he had been chronically ill since childhood. In 1720, he traveled to London to consult Dr. Richard Mead, a respected physician and admirer of his work, but the damp, smoky air of London negated the benefits of Mead’s treatments. He returned to France, spent six months with Gersaint, and then died in 1721 at age 36 on the estate of his patron, Abbé Haranger, possibly from tuberculous laryngitis. The Abbé reported that Watteau was semi-conscious and mute during his final days, clutching a paintbrush and painting imaginary scenes in the air. His nephew Louis Joseph Watteau (son of Antoine’s brother Noël Joseph Watteau, 1689–1756) and grand-nephew François-Louis-Joseph Watteau (son of Louis) followed in his footsteps. Little known during his lifetime beyond a small circle, Watteau was rarely mentioned in contemporary art criticism, often critically. Sir Michael Levey noted that Watteau "unwittingly created the concept of the individualistic artist loyal to himself alone." While followers like Lancret and Pater depicted aristocratic romanticism, Watteau’s works anticipated an art about art, viewed through an artist’s eyes, with a tone of sympathy, wistfulness, and sadness over the fleeting nature of love and joy. Walter Pater famously wrote: "He was always a seeker after something in the world, that is there in no satisfying measure, or not at all." Watteau was a prolific draftsman, typically using the *trois crayons* technique; his drawings were collected and admired even by those who criticized his paintings, such as count de Caylus and Gersaint. In 1726 and 1728, Jean de Jullienne published etchings after Watteau’s drawings, and in 1735 a series of engravings after his paintings, *The Recueil Jullienne*, which used engraving and etching techniques similar to those of Rubens’s engravers, varied in quality depending on the engraver but was generally high and unprecedented in scope, spreading his influence across Europe and into decorative arts. Watteau’s influence on painting, decorative arts, costume, film, poetry, and music was broader than that of almost any other 18th-century artist. The "Watteau dress"—a long, sacklike dress with loose pleats from the shoulder—was named after him. According to Konody’s assessment in the Encyclopædia Britannica Eleventh Edition, Watteau’s treatment of landscapes and atmospheric backgrounds contains the seeds of Impressionism. His influence was less visible in France than in England, where J. M. W. Turner admired him. A revival of interest in Watteau began in England during the British Regency and was later recognized by the Goncourt brothers in France (Edmond de Goncourt published a catalogue raisonné in 1875) and the World of Art union in Russia. In 1984, Watteau societies were founded in Paris by Jean Ferré and in London by Dr. Selby Whittingham. A major exhibition in Paris, Washington, and Berlin commemorated the 1984 tercentenary of his birth. Since 2000, a Watteau centre has been established in Valenciennes by Professor Chris Rauseo. A catalogue raisonné of Watteau’s drawings was compiled by Pierre Rosenberg and Louis-Antoine Prat, replacing the earlier work by Sir Karl Parker and Jacques Mathey; similar projects for his paintings were undertaken by Alan Wintermute and Martin Eidelberg. From September 22 to November 29, 2009, the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibited *Watteau, Music, and Theater*, showcasing his works on opera-ballet and theater, along with musical instruments and porcelains, accompanied by a catalog (ISBN 978-0-300-15507-5). From July 12 to October 2, 2016, the Frick Collection exhibited *Watteau's Soldiers: Scenes of Military Life in Eighteenth-Century France*, highlighting his focus on the quiet, prosaic aspects of war—marches, halts, encampments—where soldiers rested, daydreamed, smoked, and played cards, with a catalog by Aaron Wile (ISBN 978-1-907-80479-3). From November 23, 2021, to February 20, 2022, The J. Paul Getty Museum exhibited *The Surprise: Watteau in the J. Paul Getty Museum*, marking the 300th anniversary of Watteau’s death and celebrating the Getty’s acquisition of *The Surprise*. From October 16, 2024, to February 3, 2025, the Louvre exhibited *A new look at Watteau: An actor with no lines—Pierrot, known as Gilles*, examining Gilles and his influence on other artists, with a catalog by Guillaume Faroult (in French) (ISBN 978-2-359-06447-6).
